EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Caranddriver ↗ Open Full Page

Respect Your Elders: The London to Brighton Car Tour, Michigan Style

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.
  • Industry observers note that more than double that if you count New Londons.
  • It has been revealed that maybe a few of you with an interest in early automobiles recognize the combination of London and Brighton from the long-running English vintage-car meet that travels between those two cities every November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

Industry observers note that more than double that if you count New Londons. There are about 30 Brightons, which I think means there are somewhere around 700 ways one could set up a London-to-Brighton antique-car run. Which, of course, is a totally normal thing to strategy, right?

It has been revealed that maybe a few of you with an interest in early automobiles recognize the combination of London and Brighton from the long-running English vintage-car meet that travels between those two cities every November. First run in 1896 by an intrepid group of early—very early—car enthusiasts, the Emancipation Run was held to mark one of the first increases in speed limits: from single digits (4 mph) to a downright scorching 14 mph.

The London-to-Brighton event, or, as it’s now known, the RM Sotheby’s London to Brighton Veteran Car Run, looks like fun, so we decided to have a go between our own London and Brighton in Michigan with some antique American cars.

See all results for used cars for sale near 19604.

Sources indicate that several things lined up well. Our course between London Township and the cute main street of Brighton was 57 miles, which is a good parallel to the U.K.’s 97-km (60-mile) route. Plenty of tree-lined country lanes connect the towns, a benefit when organizing a road trip for vehicles whose max speed may be more than 14 mph but still lags behind modern highway pace. Most key, there’s a fantastic community of early-20th-century-car collectors in Michigan, so finding folks who were willing to take out their Fords, Oldsmobiles, Pullmans, and REOs was no problem.

According to recent reports, what was a problem was finding a date. Every time I suggested a weekend, I’d get a flurry of texts and emails from the would-be participants. “So sorry,” said Mark Turner. “There’s a steam-car rally that weekend.” It might have also been Turner who couldn’t do another date because of a meet for vintage Bentleys. “I don’t know if I could do June 6th because we have an HCCA [Horseless Carriage Club of America] tour down in Georgia,” said Brent Terry, with apologies. Eventually, I just picked something and hoped a few of the crew would manage to fit it into their busy, brassy schedules.

Industry observers note that an 1865 regulation required a flagger with a red warning cloth to walk ahead of any roadgoing mechanical vehicles and limited their max speed to just 4 mph on turnpikes and highways and 2 mph in cities, towns, and villages in the United Kingdom. The law was initially intended to apply to steam-powered road locomotives, which were growing in popularity in England and threatening traditional railways. As cars entered the chat, drivers chafed at the restrictions. An 1896 act of Parliament brought that speed limit up to 14 mph and was thus celebrated by English motoring clubs with a 60-mile rally, an annual tradition now under the 60-mile-long name of RM Sotheby’s London to Brighton Veteran Car Run.

See all results for used cars for sale near 19604.

Michigan being Michigan, the day before our run brought pouring rain. It turns out vintage-car people are shockingly willing to brave weather. “I believe it rains a lot in England,” said Rick Lindner. So, we highlighted up, as did eight shining examples of the earliest entries in American motoring, from a 1904 Ford Model AC owned by Lindner to a late-model 1913 Buick Model 31 helmed by Larry and Joyce Schramm. On the Car and Driver side, we brought doughnuts, passengers, and a lot of questions about old cars.

It has been revealed that after the third time I asked someone for the cubic-inch displacement of their engine, John Grace (who organizes his own vintage-car run in the fall and lent his 1911 Regal to teenage brothers Jonathan and Matthew Sinclair for our tour, and whose wife, Dorothy, once drove a Model T across America, making either one of the Graces very qualified to tell me what’s what in prewar car stuff) shook his head. He told me that while he can go look it up for me, owners of cars from this era don’t generally describe their engines in displacement. “We measure in horsepower,” he said. “I never hear anybody ask about cubic inches for early cars.”.

According to recent reports, it makes sense. In the modern era, cubic inches tend to reflect power output, but back in the days when a Curved Dash Oldsmobile might have a single jug measuring 95 cubic inches and making only four horsepower, it was more useful to announce your car’s 30 horsepower than, say, its 200 cubic inches.

Grace answered this, and all my other questions, with thoughtful enthusiasm, which is something I noticed about all the antique-car people I met that day.

Industry observers note that “The older the cars, the nicer the people,” said Larry Schramm. For the hobby to have a future, he said, it needs younger people to ask questions and learn how to drive these cars. Plus, “we’re all in the same boat.” If your car isn’t the one broken on this run, it might be on the next.

Sources indicate that antique-car drives are a bit like off-roading; it’s best to go in pairs so someone can pick you up and get you to the finish. That happened to Ted O’Dell, when his 1913 Buick Model 31 started running a temperature. When I talked to him about it, he was unbothered. Breakdowns are just a part of the process, as they were when the cars were fresh. It’s historically accurate to get a flat tire.

Sources indicate that even though I’d invited people through different contacts, most of the participants knew one another. Many of these owners have multiple cars, maybe a massive four-door for longer tours and a Model T for local runabouts. They loan one another parts and cars and smudgy business cards for the one place that still sells horsehair upholstery stuffing.

Recent findings suggest that we all gathered in a parking lot across the street from Darana Dragway. The vehicle owners hunched over crank starters to coax engines into action amid a chorus of grunts and pops, both mechanical and human. Clouds of tire smoke drifted over from the drag-strip side as smooth-bodied race machines revved big V-8s to numbers that would reduce our two- and four-cylinders to steaming puddles of Babbitt. As an example of divergent evolution, it was stark, but a show of mutual interest implied that while the bodies and power outputs were different, there was a shared soul among us.

Once our great eight were puffing and clattering, we left the dragsters behind in our own clouds of smoke (oil, not tire). I rode in David Liepelt’s 1915 Model T Ford at the head of the line. For Liepelt and his T, this marks a return to C/D. They were the stars of our Model T versus Model S story back in February 2014, and Liepelt is still mad that then–tech director Don Sherman beat his Ford in a Tesla, so we let him lead the tour.

Industry observers note that liepelt set off at a pace that would have shaken the drivers of 1896. He was all limbs, pulling the throttle lever back to full acceleration, upping the spark advance, rocking the gear-selecting pedal into high, and adjusting his Ruckstell two-speed axle. It was like watching an octopus drive a car. I had to tell him to slow down to make sure we didn’t leave anyone behind. It’s impressive what 22 horsepower is capable of, and while acceleration wasn’t going to be the challenge, nobody in the early 1900s was much for a panic stop. “Not good, but better than nothing,” Liepelt said as he barreled through an Ann Arbor intersection. If we were braking, I wasn’t aware. A line in my notebook reads, “It’s a very specific thrill to be in a car you could fall out of.”.

Thinking of joining the antiques road show? Here’s what to buy.

In a recent development, affordability was a theme among the group, which may come as a surprise to people who’ve grown up hearing terms like “Brass Era” and “prewar” only in relation to megabuck Bugattis and Duesenbergs on concours lawns. Those cars still command major prices, but more common brands have come down as older owners die and pass on to their family a garage full of acetylene headlamps and wood-spoke wheels. Our group was unanimous in suggesting a Model T as a gateway drug, including lensman James Lipman, who is now on his second T purchase (the first is shown above).

“The Brass Era ones may be worth $15,000 to $20,000,” said T owner Brent Allen. “But you can pick up a running T for sometimes $7000, $8000 easily.” Learning to drive a Model T is a challenge, but Allen said that shouldn’t put anyone off. Other owners will be eager to teach you, and there are so many reproduction parts. If you have a frame and an engine block, you can build a whole car from catalogs.

In a recent development, that thrill was a recurring theme. It’s the caress of wind in your hair like the first time you rode a bicycle. It’s the nervy pleasure of sitting the canter on a horse. It’s the very real possibility that you’ll never be able to stop. In a world where most cars can hit 100 mph before the end of an on-ramp, it’s amazing how exciting 35 mph can be when it takes all your extremities and maybe one or two of your passenger’s to keep the vehicle out of the nearest hedge.

In a recent development, for Jonathan Sinclair, the youngest of our drivers at 16, learning on a vintage car ruined him for modern transportation. When he was told that he couldn’t take the driver’s test in the family Model T, his mom had to force him to do his remaining training hours in a newer car. “I don’t feel anything!” he complained. “After the involved process of driving an older car, you get in a modern car, and suddenly you don’t have to worry about anything. It feels odd.” He and his brother, Matthew, had been planning to bring their own project, a 1911 Brush, but then the Graces offered them the key to the Regal.

Sources indicate that our summer intern, Alayna Wilkening, joined the Sinclair brothers in the Regal, where she was given the job of watching the MotoMeter hood ornament for signs of overheating. Her official report was they experienced no difficulties aside from having to explain to multiple onlookers that the Regal was a Regal but not a Buick.

Sources indicate that behind them, senior news editor Caleb Miller was riding in luxurious and secure comfort, cushioned in the azure-blue cabin of Daniel Coffman’s 1910 Pullman. I noticed with no small amount of jealousy that he had a nice sturdy roof support bar to hold on to in the turns. His post-run report was that his desire to purchase a vehicle of this vintage has only increased with each exposure. He also rode back with Liepelt and declared the trip “probably the most exhilarating 53 mph I’ve ever experienced.”.

Editor-in-chief Tony Quiroga was spared the terror of Liepelt’s sporty T, instead getting the full touring-car experience in Wes Raynard’s flashy red 1909 Oldsmobile Model X3, which cost about $2000 when it was upcoming. “This is the only one known to still exist,” Raynard told me. A quick look at past auction prices indicates that the cherry Olds changed hands earlier this year for $55,105, which is considerably more than its original purchase price but a downright bargain to own a one-of-one survivor.

Recent findings suggest that “The ride is so smooth,” Quiroga told me at our rest stop. He looked mildly disappointed that things were going so well. “I was expecting the adventure to be more adventurous. All of these enthusiasts know their cars so well that they could tear down the entire thing and rebuild it on the side of the road. Only everything is working, and we’re ahead of schedule.”.

Despite Quiroga’s desire for more chaos, the overall consensus was that the inaugural C/D London-to-Brighton (Michigan) was a great success, and the gang plans to do it again in 2027. Barring any conflicts with the steam-car rally.

It has been revealed that like a sleeper agent activated late in the game, Elana Scherr didn’t know her calling at a young age. Like many girls, she planned to be a vet-astronaut-artist, and came closest to that last one by attending UCLA art school. She painted images of cars, but did not own one. Elana reluctantly got a driver’s license at age 21 and discovered that she not only loved cars and wanted to drive them, but that other people loved cars and wanted to read about them, which meant somebody had to write about them. Since receiving activation codes, Elana has written for numerous car magazines and websites, covering classics, car culture, technology, motorsports, and fresh-car reviews. In 2020, she received a Best Feature award from the Motor Press Guild for the C/D story "A Drive through Classic Americana in a Polestar 2."  In 2023, her Car and Driver feature story "In Washington, D.C.'s Secret Carpool Cabal, It's a Daily Slug Fest" was awarded 1st place in the 16th Annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards by the Los Angeles Press Club.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light proposal for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

Recent findings suggest that this, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Sources indicate that understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s latest ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we initiative for today, tomorrow, and the future.”.

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Industry observers note that future releases, of course, include latest The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.).

It has been revealed that I don't want to write about video games any more, I want to deliver milk in the countryside and hang out with a cow and quirky people! Sorry, what, there's a game all about that called Milki Delivery that came out today? Alright, I'll write about video games again, especially when they look as charming as this one does.

It has been revealed that the stakes at play in Milki Delivery are very low (as are the steaks, no butchery to be found here, only one very sweet looking cow I couldn't possibly slaughter). You play as Neha, and she's made a promise to her pet cow, the titular Milki, that you'll find her a friend (I think this is a world where there aren't any cows left; yikes!). To do that, all you have to do is deliver her milk! Accept because this is an adventure game, you'll have to help out a few folks along the way.

Sources indicate that it's a game very much about the journey, as when riding about this lush and bright countryside, you might find a group of cats that just need a little taste of that sweet creamy juice you've got. Or maybe you have some rope that a farmer needs to wrassle up some sheep. Sometimes you'll have to get a bit more involved with the various people you meet, but predominantly, you'll be delivering milk to folks who need it.

Industry observers note that getting around the place is quite simple too, you plot out your path ahead of time and let the game take you as it's all mouse driven. A relaxed experience to be sure, but the game's art is just so delightful to look at, I'm quite enticed by the idea of just slowing down and enjoying some pretty pictures and making friends along the way. You can make different kinds of milk, too, just be feeding Milki different ingredients. Not how that works in real life, but now I kind of wish it was.

In any case, Milki Delivery is out now, and you can pick it up on Steam.

Tech Report: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that robotic technology can help surgeons perform knee replacement operations with greater precision, but that accuracy does not necessarily translate into better results for patients.
  • It has been revealed that robotic technology is becoming increasingly common in knee replacement surgery around the world.
  • The UK-wide RACER-Knee trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) in partnership with Stryker, the manufacturer of the robotic equipment evaluated in the study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that robotic technology can help surgeons perform knee replacement operations with greater precision, but that accuracy does not necessarily translate into better results for patients. The RACER-Knee trial, the world's largest clinical study of its kind, found that patients who underwent robot-assisted knee replacement experienced similar levels of pain, mobility, and recovery to those who received conventional surgery. The findings provide important evidence about the use of robotics in health care and highlight where future technological developments and research could make a difference. Coordinated by the University of Warwick and University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust, the trial was published in The Lancet, the world's oldest and one of its best-known general medical journals.

It has been revealed that robotic technology is becoming increasingly common in knee replacement surgery around the world. It is now used in 6% of procedures in the UK, 16% in the US, and 42% in Australia. The technology is designed to help surgeons position artificial knee joints more accurately and customize procedures to suit each patient's anatomy.

The UK-wide RACER-Knee trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) in partnership with Stryker, the manufacturer of the robotic equipment evaluated in the study. The Warwick Clinical Trials Unit, UHCW NHS Trust, and the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital in Birmingham led the research. It represents the world's largest double-blinded, randomized controlled trial comparing traditional total knee replacement with procedures performed using the Stryker Mako robotic system, the most widely used system of its kind worldwide.

Greater Precision Does Not Improve Recovery.

Recent findings suggest that twelve months after surgery, patients in both groups reported comparable recovery, mobility, and pain levels. Although the robotic system enabled surgeons to operate with greater precision, patients did not experience measurable improvements in their overall outcomes during the first year. The researchers also found no increased risk of serious adverse events associated with robotic assistance, suggesting that it was as safe as conventional surgery.

The trial was jointly led by two chief investigators in the UK.

Professor Andrew Metcalfe, of Warwick Medical School at the University of Warwick and a consultant orthopedic surgeon at UHCW NHS Trust, said: "We are delighted to have completed this world-leading randomized trial of an exciting technology that is now being used globally and at scale. It is an crucial step in the process of innovation and will stimulate lots more high-quality studies. We are very grateful for the support of the many patients who took part which is so important, but also the NIHR and Stryker for working so well together to support this critical study. Technology such as this could really help the care we give for patients, but for robotic-assisted knee replacements, there is still work to do before we see benefits such as less pain or better movement.".

In a recent development, professor Edward Davis, a consultant orthopedic surgeon at The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and honorary professor at the University of Birmingham, said: "The trial demonstrates robotic-arm-assistance allows for higher precision, and in theory the system should allow surgeons to customize the procedure according to a patient's anatomy. These results are by no means a condemnation of the robotic systems, but more understanding of the ideal position for a knee replacement and personalization for each patient is needed. We'll then be able to truly take advantage of the advanced precision of robotic systems.".

According to recent reports, professor Anthony Gordon, director of the NIHR Health Technology Assessment (HTA) Programme, mentioned: "Innovation in healthcare depends on evaluating promising technologies rigorously and at scale. While this study shows robotic-assisted knee replacement is not yet improving patient outcomes, it highlights opportunities to refine these technologies and harness their precision to deliver better care in the future. The NIHR continues to fund robust studies, such as RACER, ensuring we learn how to deliver the latest technologies most effectively within the NHS.".

How Robotic Knee Replacement Works.

Total knee replacement is among the most frequently performed elective surgical procedures worldwide for people with knee arthritis. During traditional surgery, orthopedic surgeons use standard surgical instruments and rely on their training and experience to position the artificial joint.

Robotic technology offers an alternative approach in which the surgeon controls a robotic arm during the operation. The system helps position surgical instruments with exceptional accuracy and allows surgeons to adjust the angles and depths of their cuts with greater flexibility. These capabilities make it possible to customize procedures to individual anatomy in ways that are not achievable with conventional techniques.

Landmark Trial Finds Similar Patient Outcomes.

The study involved 339 patients treated by 33 surgeons at 10 hospitals across the UK. Despite the potential advantages of robotic technology, researchers found no meaningful difference between the two groups in the trial's primary outcome measure, the Forgotten Joint Score, one year after surgery.

Sources indicate that this assessment measures how conscious patients are of their artificial joint while carrying out everyday activities. Ideally, a successful knee replacement allows patients to go about their daily lives without frequently noticing the artificial joint. Patients achieved similar scores regardless of which surgical technique was used.

Recent findings suggest that other measures also demonstrated comparable results. These included walking ability, pain during hospitalization, pain during the first three months of recovery and at 12 months, and the likelihood of requiring another operation.

Researchers plan to monitor participants for ten years to determine whether differences between the two surgical approaches emerge over a longer period. One particularly crucial question is whether robotic assistance reduces the number of patients who eventually need additional knee surgery.

Robotic Knee Surgery Takes Longer and Costs More.

Operations performed with robotic assistance required additional time (on average 10.5 minutes) and cost approximately £950 more per procedure.

Although the robotic system improved surgical precision, it was not associated with a higher risk of serious adverse events, indicating that the procedure appeared to be as safe as traditional knee replacement.

However, when assessed against current NHS spending thresholds, the robotic technology evaluated in the trial was not considered cost-effective during the first year following surgery.

The Future of Personalized Knee Replacement.

The researchers believe that robotic technology could become more valuable if surgeons learn how to use its enhanced precision to better accommodate differences in individual patients' anatomy.

Determining the ideal placement of an artificial knee joint for each patient could eventually allow surgeons to turn greater technical accuracy into meaningful improvements in recovery, pain relief, and mobility. Achieving those benefits will require further technological development and additional research, making personalized robotic surgery a promising area for future investigation.

The findings of the RACER-Knee trial were published in The Lancet.

The research was organized by University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust and the University of Warwick. Funding was provided by the UK NHS research organization, the National Institute for Health Research, through its Health Technology Assessment Programme (NIHR128768).

Stryker, the firm that manufactures the robotic system, covered the additional expenses associated with performing robotic surgery during the trial. The company did not participate in analyzing or interpreting the study results.

Materials provided by University of Warwick. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After becoming the world’s first all-electric 40 ton class articulated haul truck into regular series production earlier this year, the Volvo A40 has finally reached its first customers in the UK – and they wasted no time putting the substantial BEV to work on one of the nation’s largest, most key infrastructure projects.

More than sixty years after Volvo’s “Gravel Charlie” invented the articulated hauler, Volvo CE has delivered four customer A40 Electric articulated haul trucks to BMJV (a joint venture between Bouygues Travaux Publics and J Murphy & Sons) for use on the Lower Thames Crossing, further demonstrating that zero-emission machines are ready to move material at scale at major job sites right now.

It has been revealed that “Going electric today is no longer about compromise, it’s about the benefits,” explains Shaun Pidcock, Lower Thames Crossing Programme Director at BMJV. “These remarkable machines show that even the heaviest jobs can be done cleanly, and in a way that is better for those working on or living near our sites.”.

It has been revealed that the Lower Thames Crossing project is approximately 14.3 miles long, and includes more than 2.5 miles of tunnels criss-crossing beneath the River Thames. Once finished, the project will connect the Kent and Essex meters, and promises to nearly double road capacity across the east side of London while becoming the first major infrastructure program in Britain completed with carbon-neutral construction.

By using the next generation of construction machinery to make the Lower Thames Crossing Britain’s greenest road today, we are helping the industry set a fresh standard for tomorrow and make diesel-powered sites a thing of the past.

Industry observers note that since grid power isn’t available on site, BMJV is using fuel cell generators fueled by British-manufactured green hydrogen to charge the A40s. The generators produce no exhaust emissions and are noticeably quieter than combustion machines, further improving living and working conditions for the humans around the site.

Sources indicate that the “40” in the A40 Electric’s badge refers to the truck’s whopping 40 ton (39 tonne) payload capacity. Once loaded up, the hauler’s 350 kW (about 470 hp) electric motor sends power through a torque-amplifying gear reduction gearbox that, depending on how you do the math, delivers some 200,000 lb-ft of “at the wheel” torque. More than enough twisting force, in other words, to match the performance of diesel and possibly enough to have a measurable impact on the rotational speed of a planet.

That motor draws power from a 540 kWh li-ion battery good for up to six hours of continuous operation, but the hauler’s advanced regenerative braking system usually collects enough energy during operation to make it good for a full day’s shift. And, if there’s a Circle K nearby, operators can plug their A40 Electric into a 350 kW DC fast charger and get their battery from 10% to 90% in about an hour.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that even though Toyota’s Hilux pickup truck is not sold on this side of the Pacific, most people have a pretty good idea about what it represents. Thanks to the antics in Top Gear in which they were drowned, blown up, and even set on fire, the Hilux has a reputation for being rugged to the point of near indestructibility. What you don’t expect is for them to be fast.

According to recent reports, of course, things are completely different in Southeast Asia, especially in Thailand. There, a pickup truck isn’t just a rough-and-tumble tool for work, it’s also a canvas for personal expression. Thai customizers turn their trucks into insane builds that would rival anything you’d find at Daikoku Parking Area in Japan or on the floor in Vegas at SEMA.

See all results for used cars for sale near 75217.

Industry observers note that to put an exclamation point on the launch of its latest Hilux Travo Z Edition, Toyota turned to its Australian design department. Stated department reacted, to use the proper antipodean expression, by going off like a frog in a sock, building a Hilux that’s so crazy it’s not even really a pickup truck any more.

The Hyper Z prototype features massively wide bodywork that struggles to contain 325/35 series tires on 22-inch wheels, and more aerodynamic elements than a small regional airport. There’s a table-sized front splitter, a diffuser out back, ground effects tucked under the body, and a park bench of a wing out back.

Recent findings suggest that also out back, an X-shaped wing that occupies the entirety of the pickup truck’s bed. Planning a run to your local DIY center? Whatever you’re picking up better fit in the glovebox.

Sources indicate that the standard Hilux Travo is powered by a 2.4-liter turbo-diesel engine good for 150 horsepower, but despite what looks like a huge Hilux-branded intercooler here, Toyota didn’t put any power numbers on the prototype. It’s more a love letter to Thailand’s custom truck culture, showing what can be done rather than what should be done.

In a recent development, perhaps of more interest in a practical sense is how Toyota positions its Hilux in this market. Overseas, the truck is offered in both a high-floor and low-floor model, the latter riding low so that it is easier to load and unload for practical working conditions.

Industry observers note that conversely, in the U.S. market, pickups of all sizes have never been taller, which you’ll notice as soon as you need to load them up. Could Toyota successfully market a low-floor Tacoma model, one that’s a little easier to live with for commercial applications?

Either way, the Hyper Z Prototype is a cool way to shine a light on a slice of automotive culture that’s specific to a region. If you thought authentic Thai green curry was hot, just check out how spicy the country likes its pickup trucks.

10 Great Games That Defined The Nintendo Wii

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 20 years ago, Nintendo rolled out one of their most ambitious consoles of all time with the motion control-focused and internet connected Nintendo Wii.
  • According to recent reports, designed to be the most accessible console ever made for its era, the Wii became one of Nintendo’s greatest success stories.
  • However, Nintendo’s resurgence and the Wii’s global popularity wouldn’t have occurred had it not been for the wide variety of exclusive games that launched on the console and went on to define the Wii as well as Nintendo’s future prospects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

20 years ago, Nintendo rolled out one of their most ambitious consoles of all time with the motion control-focused and internet connected Nintendo Wii.

According to recent reports, designed to be the most accessible console ever made for its era, the Wii became one of Nintendo’s greatest success stories. Its easy to understand controls created a phenomenon of people of all ages getting into console gaming for the first time, from children to senior citizens.

However, Nintendo’s resurgence and the Wii’s global popularity wouldn’t have occurred had it not been for the wide variety of exclusive games that launched on the console and went on to define the Wii as well as Nintendo’s future prospects.

It has been revealed that when people think of gaming rivalries, most people will think of the console wars between Nintendo and Sega in the 1980s and 1990s. While that conflict ended with the failure of the Sega Dreamcast, the two gaming brands’ mascots wouldn’t officially meet until 2007’s Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games.

Made to coincide with the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing, Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games was the first official crossover between the Super Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog franchises, with characters from both properties being able to compete in archery, fencing, rowing, and other Olympic events.

Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games not only represents the growing comradery between Nintendo and other video game publishers but also how much pure, simplistic fun can be had on the Wii by being able to play as some of gaming’s greatest icons in jovial sports competitions.

One of the best series of games to debut with the Wii was Shigeru Miyamoto's “Wii Project” which was a series of typically Mii-centric games tailored to showcase the Wii’s controls and accessibility to more casual gamers. One of the best of these games being Wii Play.

A Wii launch title for European and Asian markets, Wii Play was essentially a Mario Party-like compilation of minigames designed to highlight the versatility of the Wiimote in games such as the Duck Hunt-like Shooting Range, Billiards, Fishing, Find Mii, and more.

Industry observers note that on a more personal note, my favorite of these minigames was the top-down Atari Combat-like Tanks! which has one or two players control tanks through toy block stages to destroy enemy tanks using the Wiimote’s D-pad.

It has been revealed that in 2006, Nintendo revolutionized mobile 2D side-scrolling Super Mario games with the release of New Super Mario Bros. for the Nintendo DS. To capitalize on that game’s success, Nintendo decided to create a multiplayer, console-based sequel, in the form of 2009’s New Super Mario Bros. Wii.

Industry observers note that the first new console-based 2D Mario game since 1995’s Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island, New Super Mario Bros. Wii was a near perfect translation of New Super Mario Bros. enhanced platforming gameplay to the Wii, with the added bonus of four-player local co-op featuring Mario, Luigi, Blue Toad, and Yellow Toad.

In a recent development, in fact, Latest Super Mario Bros. Wii might have been too perfect of a game, as Nintendo essentially kept on remastering it for years on end until the release of Super Mario Bros. Wonder. The former game was essentially ported to the Wii U and Nintendo Switch in the form of New Super Mario Bros. U, New Super Luigi U, and New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe.

Many new exclusive games made their debut on the Wii, but arguably the most creative and cinematic of them was Monolith Soft’s third-person action role-playing game Xenoblade Chronicles.

In a recent development, A spinoff of the long-running Xeno series, Xenoblade Chronicles is set in a sci-fi fantasy world where life eventually evolved on two titanic robots, the Bionis and the Mechonis, that have laid dormant for millennia. The situation led to lifeforms from both robots fighting each other in perpetual wars.

While Xenoblade Chronicles may not have been the best looking RPG on the market in 2010, it more than made up for its blurry visuals with its enthralling narrative, centered around the orphaned hero Shulk and his mysterious Monado sword, as well as its more open-world structured gameplay.

In a recent development, ever since Nintendo released the hit fighting game Super Smash Bros. Melee on the GameCube, expectations were high for its sequel. While many players would consider Super Smash Bros. Brawl to be a disappointing sequel, it still managed to delight series newcomers in many ways.

Like previous Super Smash Bros. titles, Super Smash Bros. Brawl is a crossover fighting game pitting Nintendo’s most famous characters against each other. Brawl innovated upon the series in many ways, such as featuring non-Nintendo characters like Sonic and Snake as well as featuring a stage builder.

However, what really made Brawl an epic game in the eyes of many Wii fans was its cinematic campaign, The Subspace Emissary. It depicts many of gaming's most celebrated icons fighting and joining forces together to defeat the united destructive forces of Bowser, Ganondorf, Master Hand, and Tabuu.

It's rare for video game series to never have a bad entry, especially one as long as Mario Kart, but the hit racing series has consistently managed to release banger after banger. In 2008, the Mario Kart game everybody needed to have was Mario Kart Wii.

The follow-up to the hit Mario Kart DS, Mario Kart Wii was innovative for the series in many ways, as it featured 24 player characters including customized Miis, motorcycles, and was the first home console MK game to feature online multiplayer.

In a recent development, what made Mario Kart Wii especially fun and the second best-selling Wii game was its Wii Wheel accessory. While it didn’t alter gameplay in any way, the Wii Wheel helped immerse players into the feeling of actually racing with friends online and in-person.

In the same vein as Wii Play, Shigeru Miyamoto strove to expand upon his “Wii Project” in 2007 by creating a game that would encourage families to exercise. He more or less succeeded with Wii Fit.

Primarily played through the packed-in Wii Balance Board, Wii Fit is a fairly relaxing exercise video game centered around players practicing yoga poses, strength training, aerobics, and balance on the Board, with the game further tracking people’s weight and fitness progress.

Wii Fit certainly didn’t make anyone exceptionally strong, but it did motivate millions of people to become more invested in their overall health, and it did lead many friends and family to start exercising together consistently.

Recent findings suggest that while Wii Fit didn’t make most players work up a sweat, Ubisoft Paris’ music rhythm game Just Dance certainly did, and laid the groundwork for the Wii’s longest running support. Just Dance titles would release for the console well into the eighth and ninth console generations.

Initially a Wii exclusive series, Just Dance was an expansion upon dance pad games like Dance Dance Revolution, instead having players mirror the moves of on-screen dancers as best as possible with the Wiimote tracking players' motions.

While Just Dance 1 only had a modest tracklist of 33 songs that could be played across four similar modes, it laid the groundwork for a dancing video game phenomenon that’s still going strong today; one of Ubisoft and Nintendo’s most popular series among casual and hardcore gamers alike.

At Space World 2000, Nintendo publicly revealed the Super Mario 128 project as a GameCube tech demo, featuring 128 Marios running around a spherical surface. While much of this project would be utilized in Pikmin, it wasn’t fully realized until the release of 2007’s Super Mario Galaxy.

The third 3D Super Mario game, Super Mario Galaxy was one of the most ambitious entries in the franchise, as not only did it feature a more cinematic storyline centered around Rosalina and the star-like Lumas, but had players travel across the galaxy on spherical planetoids.

This game design may have been nauseating for some players, but Super Mario Galaxy continued to show how the 3D Mario titles always strive to innovate upon each other to deliver creative, generation-defining experiences. The game even went on to directly inspire The Super Mario Galaxy Movie.

Without a doubt, the game that best defined the fun to be had on the Wii was arguably the greatest launch title of all time, Wii Sports.

The first entry in Shigeru Miyamoto's “Wii Project”, Wii Sports was a rather simplistic collection of sports games centered around customizable Miis playing tennis, baseball, bowling, golf, and boxing, in single-player or up to four-player local co-op.

However, Wii Sports’ simplistic design worked to its favor, as it allowed gamers of all ages and walks of life to easily play the game. The likes of Wii Sports bowling and tennis still being played by thousands of gamers worldwide 20 years later, in their original forms and within upcoming titles in the series.

#168042. Latest Update: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong

Latest Update: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, research has established that loneliness can have serious consequences for physical health.
  • Published in Social Problems, the study examines how chronic loneliness and social isolation became recognized as major public health concerns after researchers uncovered links to illness, premature death, and increased healthcare spending.
  • Previous studies highlighted in the research illustrate the severity of these consequences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, research has established that loneliness can have serious consequences for physical health. However, a new University of Michigan study warns that treating loneliness primarily as a health problem could shift responsibility away from society and place it on a healthcare system that lacks the tools to restore meaningful social connections.

Published in Social Problems, the study examines how chronic loneliness and social isolation became recognized as major public health concerns after researchers uncovered links to illness, premature death, and increased healthcare spending.

Previous studies highlighted in the research illustrate the severity of these consequences. One estimated that lacking social connections could be as harmful to health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Another found that loneliness, social isolation, and living alone were each associated with an approximately 30% higher risk of premature death. The financial burden is also substantial, with separate research estimating that social isolation costs Medicare $6.7 billion each year in care for older adults.

"Once people saw these findings, they began to treat loneliness as urgent," mentioned University of Michigan doctoral student Sofia Hiltner. "But it made me wonder: Why do we only consider problems key once they are tied to health?".

The Problem With Medicalizing Loneliness.

To understand how loneliness became a medical concern, Hiltner conducted interviews with experts and reviewed more than a decade of media coverage, medical journal articles, and academic literature.

Her analysis revealed that establishing a connection between loneliness and poor health helped the concern gain credibility. However, it also encouraged what she describes as a "logical leap": the belief that any problem affecting human health should become the responsibility of the healthcare system.

"Not everything that relates to health belongs in healthcare," she stated. "Doctors can screen patients and connect them to services, but they cannot rebuild communities or shorten work hours.".

Hiltner, a predoctoral trainee in social demography at the Population Studies Center within the University of Michigan's Institute for Social Research, was inspired to investigate loneliness after witnessing her grandmother become increasingly isolated as she aged.

When Hiltner entered graduate school to research social isolation among older adults, she learned that clinical trials were investigating a "loneliness pill." The discovery prompted her to question why loneliness was being approached primarily as a medical condition rather than a social problem.

"After my grandfather died, my grandmother lived alone and there was little structure in her life," Hiltner mentioned. "She didn't seem to have many friends or activities. It made me think about everything that happened throughout her life that led to that point. I wondered about the social policies, in addition to dynamics at the family level, that could have helped prevent that situation.".

Finding Solutions Beyond the Healthcare System.

Interestingly, Hiltner found that the medical community was initially reluctant to take responsibility for addressing loneliness. Much of the momentum behind incorporating loneliness into healthcare instead came from academic researchers, government health officials, and insurance companies.

Although recognizing loneliness as a medical concern can generate greater awareness and encourage intervention, it may also divert valuable resources from efforts to address the social circumstances that leave people isolated.

"There is the risk that defining loneliness as medical crowds out other ways of responding to the problem," she said. "Attention, time and resources are limited. On the other hand, framing it as medical may inspire more action than would have otherwise happened.".

Hiltner hopes her findings will encourage policymakers to reconsider how they define social problems and explore preventive strategies that address their underlying causes before they develop into serious health concerns.

In a recent development, "I would like them to reflect on the strengths and limitations of addressing problems through the healthcare system, and look farther upstream to understand how a problem emerges, considering ways to intervene before it occurs," she stated. "Healthcare can help, but it can only go so far.".

Materials provided by University of Michigan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#168041. One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1321 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that regular physical activity has long been recognized as a way to help protect against dementia.
  • In a recent development, an analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that recreational activities such as walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports were associated with a significantly lower risk of dementia.
  • Published in The Lancet Public Health, the study is the first systematic investigation into whether a phenomenon known as the "physical activity paradox" also applies to dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that regular physical activity has long been recognized as a way to help protect against dementia. However, upcoming research from the University of Southern California (USC) suggests that the circumstances in which people are physically active may be just as key as the amount of activity they get.

In a recent development, an analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that recreational activities such as walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports were associated with a significantly lower risk of dementia. Surprisingly, people who engaged in higher levels of physical activity at work appeared to face an increased risk of developing the condition.

Published in The Lancet Public Health, the study is the first systematic investigation into whether a phenomenon known as the "physical activity paradox" also applies to dementia. Already well established in cardiovascular research, this paradox refers to the observation that physical labor does not necessarily offer the same health advantages as recreational exercise and may even be associated with a greater risk of disease.

Led by David Raichlen, professor of biological sciences and anthropology at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences, the research team examined data from 74 cohort and case-control studies. Together, the studies included more than 4.2 million people between the ages of 45 and 93 from 30 countries. Over a median follow-up period of 10 years, researchers monitored diagnoses of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia.

Industry observers note that participants who engaged in higher levels of recreational physical activity had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with the least active individuals. Physical activity associated with household chores also appeared to offer benefits, although this finding was supported by only one study. In contrast, higher levels of physical activity at work were linked to a 20% greater risk of dementia. Physically active commuting was also associated with a modest increase in risk, but evidence for this relationship came from just two studies.

"The findings challenge the long-held assumption that 'every move counts' for brain health," mentioned Natan Feter, the study's first author, a postdoctoral fellow in Raichlen's Evolutionary Biology of Physical Activity Lab at USC and a researcher in the Graduate Program of Epidemiology at Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil).

Why Exercise and Physical Labor May Affect the Brain Differently.

Researchers often group recreational exercise, manual labor, household chores, and active commuting together when measuring "Physical activity." However, the authors suggest that the circumstances surrounding these activities vary considerably and could influence their long-term health effects.

According to recent reports, people who exercise during their free time generally have greater control over the intensity and nature of their activities. Recreational exercise can also provide opportunities to socialize and relieve stress. In comparison, physically demanding occupations may require repeated movements, extended periods of standing, heavy lifting, and insufficient time to recover, along with exposure to potentially harmful workplace conditions.

According to recent reports, the researchers do not believe that physical movement itself is likely to explain the elevated dementia risk associated with occupational activity. Instead, the relationship may arise from the social and environmental factors commonly associated with manual labor.

It has been revealed that physically demanding occupations are more likely to expose workers to psychological and social stress, limited control over their work, unsafe conditions, and higher levels of air and noise pollution. Each of these factors has independently been associated with dementia risk. Workers may also struggle to participate in recreational exercise because of exhaustion, limited free time, or a lack of access to safe spaces for physical activity.

Opposing Patterns in Dementia Risk.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between physical activity and dementia risk was not linear and followed opposite patterns depending on the type of activity.

Industry observers note that as recreational exercise increased, dementia risk gradually declined until the apparent benefits leveled off. Occupational physical activity revealed the reverse pattern, with dementia risk increasing at higher activity levels before eventually reaching a plateau.

Important Limitations and Unanswered Questions.

It has been revealed that the authors emphasize that there is still too little research on physical activity related to household chores and commuting to draw definitive conclusions about either. Most of the available evidence also comes from high-income countries, despite projections that low- and middle-income nations will experience the greatest increases in dementia cases in the coming decades.

Another limitation is that almost all the studies depended on participants reporting their own physical activity. This approach can introduce errors if people do not accurately remember their activity levels. Nevertheless, Feter mentioned the consistency of the findings across several additional statistical analyses suggests that the observed relationships warrant serious attention.

It has been revealed that the researchers stress that their findings should not discourage people from pursuing physically active occupations. Since the analysis relied on observational research, it cannot establish that occupational physical activity causes dementia.

According to recent reports, instead, the results underscore the importance of examining the conditions under which people are physically active. Recreational exercise continued to be associated with a lower risk of dementia, while occupational activity remained linked to a higher risk even after researchers accounted for differences in age, education, and chronic health conditions.

How Sedentary Activities May Also Influence Brain Health.

Recent findings suggest that the importance of context may extend beyond physical activity. Separate research by Raichlen, Feter, and their colleagues, published recently in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, suggests that different types of sedentary behavior may also be associated with differences in brain structure.

In that study, mentally stimulating activities performed while sitting, such as working at a desk, were associated with greater volume in certain regions of the cerebral cortex than more passive activities, such as watching television. These differences included brain regions involved in executive function.

Together, the findings could have notable implications for public health strategies aimed at reducing dementia risk. The authors suggest that encouraging people to "move more" may not be sufficient without also addressing the circumstances in which physical activity takes place.

Recent findings suggest that "In other words, when it comes to protecting the brain, the context of physical activity may matter just as much as movement itself," Raichlen stated. "Improving access to safe parks, walking trails and recreational facilities, ensuring people have adequate leisure time for exercise, and reducing harmful workplace exposures may ultimately prove as important as promoting physical activity itself.".

It has been revealed that raichlen and Feter's co-authors include Tiladia Markarian, Dylan M. Luong, Jack Gunnink, Anamika Nanda, Sarah Hourihan and Ashley Ventura of USC; Eduardo Caputo, Jayne Feter, Gustavo S. Silva and Airton José Rombaldi of Universidade Federal de Pelotas (Brazil); Paula Iso-Markku of the University of Helsinki (Finland); Daniela Benzano Bumaguin of Fundação Universitária de Cardiologia (Brazil); Yann C. Klimentidis and Gene E. Alexander of the University of Arizona; Daniel Umpierre and Natália Schröder of Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil); and Pedro C. Hallal of University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Dually Noted: The Reasons Why Some Pickup Trucks and Vans Come with Dual Rear Wheels

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the term “dual rear wheels,” as applied to full-size pickup trucks and vans, raises as many questions as it answers.
  • You’ll often see so-equipped vehicles referred to in official specs or on a build sheet as DRW, as opposed to single-rear-wheel (SRW) pickups and vans.
  • DRW vans are usually the longest and tallest, used for both cargo and passenger hauling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the term “dual rear wheels,” as applied to full-size pickup trucks and vans, raises as many questions as it answers. Namely, one: Don’t all vehicles have two rear wheels? Good work, detective. The dual part, however, refers to the number of rear wheels on each side. Confusing? Sure. But consider yourself a member of an elite club. Send away for your decoder ring now.

You’ll often see so-equipped vehicles referred to in official specs or on a build sheet as DRW, as opposed to single-rear-wheel (SRW) pickups and vans. Out in the real world, you’re likely to observe dually pickups towing major, heavy trailers, often using a gooseneck or fifth-wheel hitch.

DRW vans are usually the longest and tallest, used for both cargo and passenger hauling. Simply put, DRW vehicles are meant to handle major loads.

Automakers go the DRW route on configurations of their heavy-duty trucks and vans designed for hauling and/or towing heavy loads. Having those extra tires means more contact patch over which to distribute the weight. It’s the same basic principle that’s used on semi trucks—having 18 or so wheels spread across the semi tractor and its trailer allows the rig to carry literal tons.

See all results for used cars for sale near 21014.

In a recent development, on dually trucks, the wider stance helps increase stability as well. You can think of the two extra wheels like outriggers, keeping the truck better planted in the face of crosswinds or in turns.

The main drawbacks of a dually setup are somewhat obvious. You have to worry about six tires instead of four, which in turn makes tire replacement more expensive. For dually trucks, the extra wheels sit outside the normal pickup-bed envelope, necessitating flared fenders to cover the extra rubber.

Maneuvering a big SRW truck or van is difficult enough. Predictably, the additional width of a DRW vehicle only adds to the challenge. It’s why many dually trucks end up with a blemish or two on at least one rear fender. The fenders of newer dually pickups are made from lighter-weight fiberglass instead of steel, so they’re less likely to bend and more prone to cracking when they meet a stationary object.

Industry observers note that this isn’t the case with most dually full-size vans. So-equipped vans add their additional tires inboard, which eliminates the need for flared rear fenders. The consequence of this arrangement is a slight reduction in outright cargo space due to the wheel wells extending further into the cabin.

Ever wonder why the front wheels of a dually truck or van have a severe outward dish to them? It’s so that all the wheels match and are therefore interchangeable should you need to use the spare. This dished design allows the rear wheels on one side to mate up with each other, which enables the use of two rear tires on both sides of the vehicle.

See all results for used cars for sale near 21014.

It has been revealed that the need for a dually comes down to capability. DRWs may be necessary to comfortably pull a fully laden horse trailer, a giant camper, various types of farm equipment, or the crops they help sow and reap. To get an idea of how much more a dually can handle, an SRW heavy-duty truck may be rated for a little more than 20,000 pounds of trailer weight on a bumper-mounted hitch, while the DRW variant of the same basic truck with a gooseneck hitch can pull almost twice the weight.

The difference isn’t as great with dual-rear-wheel versus SRW vans, mostly because both use bumper-mounted hitches. A DRW van may be able to tow as much as 50 percent more weight than a comparable SRW version. With some vans, towing capacity actually goes down when you add two rear wheels. Why go the dually route, then? Because that extra rubber is advantageous to rear-end stability—particularly when a van’s loaded up at, or near, its maximum payload capacity.

According to recent reports, dually setups are available on heavy-duty versions of full-size pickups and some large vans. Those looking for a pickup truck with a bed can choose this setup on the Chevrolet Silverado HD, GMC Sierra HD, Ram HD, and Ford F-series Super Duty.

In the realm of enclosed passenger and cargo vans, only the Ford Transit and Mercedes-Benz Sprinter offer available DRW configurations. You’ll also often find DRWs in use on cutaway and chassis-cab versions of these trucks and vans, which are used in the aftermarket to build things such as box trucks, tow trucks, and RVs.

In some international markets, where full-size pickups are much less common, automakers produce DRW versions of their sub-full-size pickups.

Sources indicate that as with any towing or hauling exercise, make sure you understand the limits of your specific vehicle before loading it up or hitching a trailer to the back. Consider what you’re likely to tow or haul when shopping for your workhorse, and follow the manufacturer’s guidance on loading so you stay safe and avoid putting too much strain on the vehicle.

Dually is a term used for a pickup truck or van with dual rear wheels (DRW).

A dually pickup truck or van has two wheels and tires on each side of its rear axle for a grand total of four rear wheels and tires.

You do not need a CDL to drive a full-size pickup truck or an enclosed cargo or passenger van with dual rear wheels (DRWs).

Pedants will note that even a rear-wheel-drive dually relies on its engine to power four wheels (the four back ones). In a technical sense, however, a rear-drive dually is a two-wheel-drive vehicle, since power is sent to the drive wheels via two axle shafts. Similarly, though a four-wheel-drive-equipped dually may power a total of six wheels, the engine’s power only reaches the drive wheels via a total of four axle shafts (two at each end).

He can parallel-park a school bus and once drove a Lincoln Town Car 63 mph in reverse. After taking a break from journalism to work on autonomous vehicles, he’s back writing for this and other automotive publications. Despite being £61.7 million in debt, bankrupt MindsEye devs Build a Rocket Boy are splurging on legal action against "a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews"

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that freshly published bankruptcy documents for perennially troubled MindsEye developer Build A Rocket Boy have spelled out the scale of the firm's debt, with around £61.7 million owed to creditors.
  • Recent findings suggest that BARB's largest debt by far is the roughly £36.5 million owed to NetEase, publishers of Marvel Rivals.
  • In a recent development, build a Rocket Boy have been on a journey, it's fair to say.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that freshly published bankruptcy documents for perennially troubled MindsEye developer Build A Rocket Boy have spelled out the scale of the firm's debt, with around £61.7 million owed to creditors. The documents also touch on founder Leslie Benzies and CEO Mark Gerhard's claims that MindsEye is the victim of an organised sabotage campaign. The company's leaders have apparently taken out even more loans in order to fund legal action against the suspected perpetrators, with the promise of a healthy payout. I'm not holding my breath.

Recent findings suggest that BARB's largest debt by far is the roughly £36.5 million owed to NetEase, publishers of Marvel Rivals. Asset manager Diameter Capital Partners are the second largest external creditor, having loaned BARB around £4.25 million. A further $19 million is owed to "group undertakings" – "group undertakings" meaning debts to parent companies, subsidiaries or fellow subsidiaries. Studio founder Benzies, meanwhile, is owed £1,158,167.05. Given that Benzies has been repeatedly accused of torpedoing MindsEye's fortunes by way of disruptive micro-management, I'm not sure many BARB staff would agree that he really deserves his million quid back at this stage, but that's what it indicates on paper. Smaller IOUs include £10,434.11 for Amazon Web Services, £634.36 for Unity, and a mighty £19.90 for OpenAI.

In a recent development, build a Rocket Boy have been on a journey, it's fair to say. Confirmed in 2023, their flagship project MindsEye is a filmic GTA-ish action shooter initially billed as a full-fat demo for Everywhere, a game creation platform comparable to Roblox. MindsEye struggled to compel us before launch and did not find its people on release, with poor sales leading to layoffs even as BARB leadership insisted they could revive the game's fortunes.

The same leadership were subsequently accused by their own staff of "disastrously" mishandling the redundancies and enforcing "unbearable" crunch. Unionised BARB employees have now taken management to court for installing alleged surveillance software on their work PCs. The game's publishers Io Interactive noped out of the picture in March this year. Meanwhile, Benzies and Gerhard have thrown around accusations of a sinister espionage and sabotage campaign, carried out by unspecified perpetrators. They made a sort of revenge fantasy DLC pack about it, which our own Mark Warren characterised as we-already-have-Hitman-at-home. The bankruptcy documents shed more light on these twists and turns. According to the administrators, BARB were "funded mainly by equity investment from institutional, strategic and venture capital investors over several funding rounds, including a $110m Series D round in 2023." This followed a £32 million investment in 2020, as reported by GI. The organization grew significantly during MindsEye's creation to around 500 UK and overseas employees. According to a group income statement, the company posted sequential operating losses of £47.5 million for the period ending September 30th, 2025, and £63.1 million for the year ending December 2024. The administrator proposals document also devotes some time to the aforesaid allegations of sabotage. "The directors formed the view that the game's commercial prospects may have been adversely affected by a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary," it reads. "The directors subsequently received information which they considered suggested the involvement of a number of third parties in organising and funding such activity and commenced litigation against some of those parties. The directors have indicated that such claims may be substantial in value, although the extent of any recovery remains uncertain and will be dependent upon the outcome of ongoing investigations, legal proceedings and asset recovery actions." A later section vaguely alludes to the sum BARB leadership hope to recover. "Prior to the Joint Administrators' appointment, the Company had undertaken detailed investigations and had commenced litigation against several third parties, with the assistance of the Company's former legal advisers, Brandsmiths, in connection with matters described earlier in the Proposals," the doc reads. "The Joint Administrators consider the litigation potentially to be the largest asset of the Administration." The document goes on that BARB management have "sought financial support from third party investors to fund the anticipated legal costs and expenses associated with the litigation", with some of these funding agreements already executed. "Further executed agreements and associated funding contributions are expected to be received, shortly, and a substantial litigation fund is anticipated to arise," it continues. The Joint Administrators are "at the moment engaging in the on-going litigation, progressing the funding arrangements entered into by the Company, and have assessed the merits of pursuing the litigation". They will liaise with relevant parties to "determine the most appropriate strategy for preserving and, where appropriate, realising value from this potential asset for the benefit of creditors and other stakeholders." The doc doesn't name who, exactly, is being taken to court. As far as I'm aware, it isn't us. Anyway, it's good to know that the company who owe over £60 million are taking on more debt in order to pursue a histrionic grievance for which they have yet to supply any real evidence whatsoever.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off.
  • In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios remarked that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead declared a delay. The at the moment ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Recent findings suggest that season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios remarked that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Recent findings suggest that given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Escalating the fight with fresh threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj.

In a recent development, what we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension revision is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

Recent findings suggest that similar to other Bonus Paths, the fresh Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several fresh customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

#168034. Industry News: A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (891 w)
📖 Baca
